questions.question: Why are in-line reciprocating engines normally limited to four or six cylinders?
questions.correct_answer: The rearmost cylinders receive very little cooling air, restricting how many cylinders can be effectively cooled.
distractors: The small frontal area creates insufficient airflow for fuel atomization beyond six cylinders.
The power-to-weight ratio becomes too high for the airframe structure beyond six cylinders.
The combustion process in the front cylinders consumes too much oxygen, starving rear cylinders beyond six.
questions.explanation: According to the PHAK Chapter 7, in-line engines have a comparatively small frontal area, but the rearmost cylinders of an air-cooled, in-line engine receive very little cooling air. This cooling limitation is what restricts these engines to four or six cylinders, not issues related to fuel atomization, structural limits, or oxygen starvation.

questions.question: A propeller blade is designed with a greater angle of incidence near the hub than at the tip. What is the primary purpose of this twist?
questions.correct_answer: To produce uniform lift from the hub to the tip by compensating for the difference in rotational speed along the blade
distractors: To reduce aerodynamic drag at the blade tips where the rotational speed is greatest
To increase structural strength of the blade near the hub where centrifugal forces are highest
To allow the propeller to maintain a constant RPM during changes in engine power output
questions.explanation: According to the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (Chapter 7), the twist in a propeller blade exists to produce uniform lift from the hub to the tip. Because the tip travels a greater distance than the hub in the same amount of time, it moves faster through the air. If the blade had a constant angle of incidence, the faster-moving tip would produce far more lift than the hub. By varying the angle of incidence to correspond with the rotational speed at each point along the blade, lift is equalized. The distractors are incorrect because the twist is an aerodynamic design for lift uniformity—not for drag reduction, structural reinforcement, or RPM governing (which is the job of a constant-speed propeller governor).

questions.question: Why would a propeller blade with the same pitch throughout its entire length be inefficient as airspeed increases in flight?
questions.correct_answer: The portion near the hub would have a negative angle of attack while the blade tip would be stalled
distractors: The portion near the hub would be stalled while the blade tip would have a negative angle of attack
The entire blade would simultaneously stall as forward airspeed increases
The portion near the hub would produce excessive thrust while the blade tip would produce no thrust
questions.explanation: According to the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (Chapter 7), a propeller blade with the same pitch throughout its entire length would be inefficient because, as airspeed increases in flight, the different rotational speeds along the blade cause the inner portion near the hub to develop a negative angle of attack while the faster-moving blade tip would stall. This is why propeller blades are designed with a twist — varying pitch along their length — to maintain an efficient angle of attack across the entire blade span.

questions.question: A pilot is flying an aircraft with a constant-speed propeller and notices a continuous decrease in airspeed. If the airspeed decreases enough to rotate the propeller blades to the low pitch stop, what will happen to engine RPM with any further decrease in airspeed?
questions.correct_answer: Engine RPM will decrease in the same manner as a fixed-pitch propeller, because the blades can no longer reduce pitch to maintain RPM
distractors: Engine RPM will remain constant because the constant-speed governor will continue to adjust blade angle regardless of the low pitch stop
Engine RPM will increase because the reduced airspeed lowers the aerodynamic load on the propeller blades
Engine RPM will remain constant because the manifold pressure automatically compensates for the airspeed loss
questions.explanation: According to PHAK Chapter 7, a constant-speed propeller maintains selected RPM by adjusting blade pitch as airspeed changes. However, once airspeed decreases enough to rotate the blades to the low pitch stop, the blades cannot decrease pitch any further. At this point, the constant-speed mechanism has reached its limit, and any additional decrease in airspeed will cause engine RPM to decrease just as it would with a fixed-pitch propeller. The governor cannot maintain RPM beyond the mechanical limits of the blade pitch range.

distractors: The blade angle can no longer increase, so engine RPM decreases just like a fixed-pitch propeller
The propeller governor reduces blade angle to prevent the engine from exceeding redline RPM
The blade angle continues to increase beyond the stop, maintaining the selected RPM

This is the opposite of the low pitch stop scenario, where a decrease in airspeed causes RPM to decrease as it would with a fixed-pitch propeller.

questions.question: Under what condition does the governor of a constant-speed propeller stop maintaining the selected engine RPM?
questions.correct_answer: When the propeller blades contact a pitch stop.
distractors: When the pilot adjusts the manifold pressure using the throttle.
When the aircraft experiences an increase or decrease in airspeed.
When the propeller control lever is adjusted to select a new RPM.
questions.explanation: According to the PHAK, a constant engine rpm is maintained by the governor as long as the propeller blade angle remains within the constant-speed range and is not against either pitch stop. The governor actively adjusts the blade angle to compensate for changes in airspeed or propeller load. However, once the propeller blades contact a high or low pitch stop, they have reached the limit of their adjustable range, and the engine rpm is no longer maintained by the governor.

questions.question: A pilot experiences a propeller failure causing the blades to move to the low pitch stop position, resulting in a propeller overspeed condition. Attempting to maintain level flight at the published best glide speed, the pilot finds inadequate thrust is being generated. What should the pilot understand about this situation?
questions.correct_answer: An airspeed lower than the published best glide speed may produce increased thrust, potentially enabling the pilot to maintain level flight
distractors: An airspeed higher than the published best glide speed would generate more thrust by increasing propeller rpm and airflow through the engine
The published best glide speed will always generate adequate thrust regardless of propeller blade position, so the pilot should focus on increasing manifold pressure instead
The only way to generate additional thrust is to reduce manifold pressure, which will slow the propeller and allow the blades to move off the low pitch stop
questions.explanation: According to PHAK Chapter 7, when propeller blades are stuck at the low pitch stop position, the propeller operates like a fixed-pitch propeller that changes rpm with changes in power and airspeed. A performance evaluation of this condition found that an airspeed lower than the published best glide speed would have resulted in increased thrust, enabling the pilot to maintain level flight. The low pitch setting is designed for maximum takeoff power but can cause propeller overspeed at higher airspeeds, meaning the published best glide speed may not be low enough to generate adequate thrust for a given propeller installation in this specific failure mode.

questions.question: A variable-pitch propeller has failed and the blades are stuck at the low pitch stop position, causing a propeller overspeed condition. According to the SAIB discussed in the PHAK, what action might enable the pilot to maintain level flight?
questions.correct_answer: Reduce airspeed below the published best glide speed to increase thrust
distractors: Increase airspeed above best glide to drive the propeller faster and generate more thrust
Maintain best glide speed, as it always provides the optimal thrust for any propeller condition
Reduce manifold pressure to minimum and accept a descent at best glide speed
questions.explanation: The PHAK describes an incident where a propeller's blade pitch change mechanism failed to the low pitch stop, causing it to act like a fixed-pitch propeller that can overspeed at higher airspeed. A performance evaluation found that an airspeed lower than best glide speed would have resulted in increased thrust, enabling level flight. This is because the published best glide speed may not be low enough to generate adequate thrust when the propeller is stuck at the low pitch stop. This counterintuitive finding illustrates that standard best glide speeds are optimized for a functioning propeller, not for this specific failure mode.

The airspeed needed for level flight will always be higher than best glide speed, requiring the pilot to increase speed.
The airspeed needed for level flight must be maintained at the stall warning horn activation to prevent further overspeed.

Pilots should be aware that some reduction in airspeed may result in the ability for continued safe flight and landing, though determining a more suitable airspeed should only be conducted at a safe altitude.

questions.question: During a propeller overspeed event, a pilot discovers that engine-out best glide speed may not provide the airspeed necessary to maintain level flight. Under what conditions should the pilot attempt to determine a more suitable airspeed?
questions.correct_answer: Only at a safe altitude when the pilot has time to determine an alternative course of action other than landing
distractors: Immediately upon recognizing the overspeed, regardless of altitude, to prevent propeller damage
Only after the engine has been secured and the propeller has stopped windmilling
At any altitude provided the aircraft is first configured for engine-out best glide speed
questions.explanation: According to PHAK Chapter 7, during a propeller overspeed the airspeed necessary to maintain level flight may be different than engine-out best glide speed, and some reduction in airspeed may allow continued safe flight and landing. However, the handbook specifically states that determining an airspeed more suitable than engine-out best glide speed should only be conducted at a safe altitude when the pilot has time to determine an alternative course of action. This emphasizes that experimenting with airspeed during an emergency requires sufficient altitude and time to avoid creating a more dangerous situation.

questions.question: When operating at high altitudes without leaning the mixture, carbon buildup can foul the spark plugs. What is the primary reason a rich mixture causes this carbon buildup?
questions.correct_answer: The rich mixture lowers the temperature inside the cylinder, inhibiting complete combustion of the fuel.
distractors: The rich mixture raises the temperature inside the cylinder, causing the fuel to burn too quickly and leave carbon residue.
The rich mixture increases the pressure inside the cylinder, preventing the spark plugs from firing consistently.
The rich mixture increases the humidity inside the cylinder, which traps carbon particles on the spark plug electrodes.
questions.explanation: According to the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (Chapter 7), at higher altitudes the density of air entering the carburetor decreases while fuel density remains the same, creating a progressively richer mixture. This rich mixture lowers the temperature inside the cylinder, which inhibits complete combustion of the fuel and leads to carbon buildup on the spark plugs. Leaning the mixture compensates for decreased air density and helps prevent this condition.

questions.question: A pilot flying an aircraft with a fixed-pitch propeller applies carburetor heat and observes the RPM drop, then gradually begin to climb back up. What does this indicate?
questions.correct_answer: Carburetor ice was present and is melting
distractors: No carburetor ice was present and the engine is running normally
The carburetor heat is malfunctioning and should be turned off immediately
The mixture has become excessively lean due to the heated air
questions.explanation: According to the PHAK Chapter 7, when ice is present in an aircraft with a fixed-pitch propeller and carburetor heat is applied, there is a decrease in RPM followed by a gradual increase in RPM as the ice melts. This distinguishes it from the no-ice condition, where RPM decreases and then remains decreased. The initial RPM drop occurs because the heated air is less dense, enriching the mixture, but as the ice melts and airflow is restored, RPM recovers. The engine should also run more smoothly once the ice has been removed.

questions.question: During a carburetor heat check on an aircraft with a constant-speed propeller, you apply carburetor heat and observe an initial decrease in manifold pressure with no subsequent gradual increase. Assuming no carburetor ice is present, when would you expect to see manifold pressure increase?
questions.correct_answer: When the carburetor heat is turned off
distractors: After a few seconds, once the warmer air stabilizes in the intake manifold
Immediately after the initial decrease, as the engine compensates for the temperature change
The manifold pressure would remain at its decreased value even after carburetor heat is turned off
questions.explanation: According to the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (Chapter 7), when carburetor heat is applied on an aircraft with a constant-speed propeller and ice IS present, the pilot sees a decrease in manifold pressure followed by a gradual increase as the ice melts. However, if carburetor icing is NOT present, that gradual increase in manifold pressure does not occur while the heat is on. The increase in manifold pressure only becomes apparent when the carburetor heat is turned off and denser, cooler air is restored to the engine.

questions.question: A pilot applies full carburetor heat to clear suspected carburetor ice. The engine runs rougher and power drops further. What is the correct pilot action during this period?
questions.correct_answer: Leave carburetor heat in the full-hot position until normal power returns
distractors: Reduce carburetor heat to partial hot to stabilize engine roughness
Remove carburetor heat temporarily to restore power, then reapply it
Cycle carburetor heat on and off in 10-second intervals to clear ice gradually
Remove carburetor heat completely and plan an immediate precautionary landing
questions.explanation: According to PHAK Chapter 7, applying full carburetor heat to clear ice will further reduce power and may cause engine roughness as melted ice passes through the engine. These symptoms can last from 30 seconds to several minutes depending on icing severity. The handbook explicitly states that during this period, the pilot must resist the temptation to decrease carburetor heat usage and must keep it in the full-hot position until normal power returns. Reducing or cycling heat would interrupt the ice-clearing process and could allow ice to re-form.

questions.question: Under what conditions may a pilot operate an engine with the carburetor air temperature indicator in the yellow arc?
questions.correct_answer: When the air temperature and moisture content are such that carburetor icing is improbable
distractors: Only during descents with reduced power settings, regardless of atmospheric conditions
Only after carburetor heat has been fully applied to warm the induction system
At any time, since the yellow arc merely indicates a cautionary temperature range with no operational restrictions
questions.explanation: According to PHAK Chapter 7, the yellow arc on the carburetor air temperature indicator represents the temperature range where carburetor icing may occur (typically -15°C to +5°C). The handbook explicitly states that if the air temperature and moisture content of the air are such that carburetor icing is improbable, the engine can be operated with the indicator in the yellow range with no adverse effects. However, if atmospheric conditions are conducive to carburetor icing, the pilot must keep the indicator outside the yellow arc by applying carburetor heat. Distractor A is incorrect because the permissibility depends on atmospheric conditions, not phase of flight. Distractor B is incorrect because applying carburetor heat is the remedy used to move the indicator OUT of the yellow arc when icing conditions exist. Distractor C is incorrect because it ignores the requirement to avoid the yellow arc when conditions are conducive to icing.

questions.question: When an aircraft equipped with a two-speed supercharger reaches the specified altitude to shift to high blower, what is the correct sequence of pilot actions?
questions.correct_answer: Make a power reduction, switch the supercharger control to high blower, and then reset the throttle to the desired manifold pressure.
distractors: Switch the supercharger control to high blower, make a power reduction, and then reset the throttle to the desired manifold pressure.
Reset the throttle to the desired manifold pressure, make a power reduction, and then switch the supercharger control to high blower.
Switch the supercharger control to high blower, reset the throttle to the desired manifold pressure, and then make a power reduction.
questions.explanation: According to the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (PHAK) Chapter 7, when an aircraft with a supercharger reaches a specified altitude, a power reduction is made first. The supercharger control is then switched to the high blower position, and finally, the throttle is reset to the desired manifold pressure.
